guide.title: East Flatbush, Brooklyn: Little Caribbean and Holy Cross
guide.intro: East Flatbush grew out of the colonial Town of Flatbush and was largely populated by Jewish and Italian residents before 1950. Substantial West Indian immigration from the 1960s onward, alongside a Black population that formed the majority by the 1990s, remade it; Wikipedia describes it as the single largest West Indian neighborhood in all of New York City and America as a whole. Holy Cross Cemetery has been here since 1849, when Bishop John Hughes bought land from the Van Brunt farm. Brooklyn Community District 17, which comprises East Flatbush and its subsections, covers 3.1 square miles and recorded a 2020 Census population of 162,446, about 78.3 percent of it Black or African American and roughly half foreign-born. The neighborhood is informally divided into three sections: Erasmus in the west, Farragut in the centre, and Remsen Village and Rugby in the east.

sections.heading: Cemetery, cultural district and three sub-sections
sections.body:
Holy Cross Cemetery was established in 1849, when Bishop John Hughes purchased land from the Van Brunt farm to relieve overcrowding at other Catholic burial grounds; the first interment was on July 13, 1849. Bishop John Loughlin later commissioned the Chapel of the Resurrection, completed in 1855, whose catacombs hold pioneer priests and members of prominent Catholic families. The cemetery grew to 96 acres and transferred to the Saint John's Cemetery Corporation in 2007. Among those buried here are the baseball figure Gil Hodges, the businessman Diamond Jim Brady, Mayor William R. Grace, Mayor and Representative Ardolph L. Kline, Representative John Michael Clancy, four Medal of Honor recipients and Samuel O'Reilly, who patented the electric tattoo machine.

On September 28, 2017, Little Caribbean was designated as a cultural district, described as the first and only officially recognised Little Caribbean in the world. It is sponsored by I AM caribBEING, founded in 2010 by the Trinidadian-descended Flatbush native Shelley Worrell, and its commercial corridors run along Flatbush, Church, Nostrand and Utica avenues, overlapping Brooklyn Community Districts 9, 14 and 17. In 2006 the stretch of Church Avenue between Remsen Avenue and East 98th Street, in the eastern part of the neighborhood, was co-named Bob Marley Boulevard. In 2021 the Newkirk Avenue station was formally renamed Newkirk Avenue-Little Haiti.

The neighborhood's three informal sub-sections carry their own names and their own histories. Farragut, in the centre, was named for the Civil War Admiral David Farragut, and holds Flatbush Gardens, a 59-building complex built in 1949 on the former site of the Flatbush Water Works. Rugby, in the east, was named by developers in the 1890s; the name survives on Rugby Road and on the Rugby branch of the Brooklyn Public Library at 1000 Utica Avenue. Remsen Village, the name that took over from Rugby, only emerged in the mid-1990s. Each has its own page here.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The IRT Nostrand Avenue Line runs along the neighborhood's Nostrand Avenue corridor. Church Avenue, at Church and Nostrand Avenues, straddles East Flatbush and Flatbush and is served by the 2 at all times and the 5 on weekdays. Beverly Road, at Beverley Road and Nostrand Avenue, straddles the same two neighborhoods with the same service. Newkirk Avenue-Little Haiti, at Newkirk and Nostrand Avenues, also straddles East Flatbush and Flatbush and is served by the 2 and the 5.

On the IRT New Lots Line, Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road sits at Sutter Avenue, Rutland Road and East 98th Street, on the border of East Flatbush and Brownsville. It is served by the 3 at all times except late nights, when the 4 takes over, with limited rush-hour 2 and 5 service.

faq.question: How do I get to East Flatbush?
faq.answer: By subway. The 2 and 5 run the IRT Nostrand Avenue Line, calling at Church Avenue, Beverly Road and Newkirk Avenue-Little Haiti, all of which straddle East Flatbush and Flatbush. On the IRT New Lots Line, Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road sits on the East Flatbush and Brownsville border and is served by the 3, with the 4 taking over late nights.

faq.question: Can I visit Holy Cross Cemetery?
faq.answer: Yes. The cemetery's own site gives visitor hours of 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM daily, with the office open weekdays 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM and Saturdays 9:00 AM to 1:00 PM by appointment, closed Sundays and holidays.

faq.question: What is Little Caribbean?
faq.answer: A cultural district designated on September 28, 2017 and described as the first and only officially recognised Little Caribbean in the world. It is sponsored by I AM caribBEING, and its commercial corridors run along Flatbush, Church, Nostrand and Utica avenues across three community districts.

faq.question: What are Farragut, Rugby and Remsen Village?
faq.answer: The three informal sub-sections of East Flatbush: Erasmus in the west, Farragut in the centre, and Remsen Village and Rugby in the east. Rugby was the developers' name from the 1890s; Remsen Village came into use only in the mid-1990s for the same ground.

faq.question: Are there hotels in East Flatbush?
faq.answer: No hotel could be confirmed as physically located within East Flatbush's commonly cited boundaries, so none is listed here. Booking results returned under the East Flatbush name point to properties in the Flatlands and Bergen Beach area instead.

photos.title: The Holy Cross Cemetery gate on Tilden Avenue
photos.description: A stone gatehouse with twin arches and a green roof, lettered Holy Cross Cemetery under a cross, snow banked at the kerb.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

photos.title: The former Congregation Beth Israel front gate
photos.description: A pale brick front with arched windows above a double wooden door, Stars of David worked into the iron gate and railings.
photos.author: Onorland

photos.title: The East Flatbush branch library
photos.description: A single-storey library front of white fluted panels above a full-width glazed shopfront, with the street reflected in the glass.
photos.author: QuasyBoy

places.name: Former Congregation Beth Israel
places.summary: A former synagogue building listed on the National Register of Historic Places on April 30, 2009, reference number 09000256. It is used today as Mt. Zion Church of God, Seventh Day, and reflects the neighborhood's earlier Jewish population.

places.address: Commercial corridors along Flatbush, Church, Nostrand and Utica Avenues, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A cultural district designated on September 28, 2017, described as the first and only officially recognised Little Caribbean in the world. It is sponsored by I AM caribBEING, founded in 2010 by Shelley Worrell, and overlaps Brooklyn Community Districts 9, 14 and 17.

places.name: Shirley Chisholm Recreation Center
places.summary: A recreation centre of roughly 74,000 square feet within Nostrand Playground, opened on February 10, 2026 and billed as the largest NYC Parks recreation centre in Brooklyn and the first in Central Brooklyn.

places.name: Paerdegat Park
places.address: 4002 Foster Avenue, Brooklyn, NY, on Albany Avenue and East 40th Street between Farragut Road and Foster Avenue
places.summary: A 3.56-acre community park in the Farragut section of East Flatbush, named after the historic Paerdegat Basin.

places.name: East Flatbush Children's Playground
places.address: 68 East 94th Street, between Rutland Road and East New York Avenue, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A small NYC Parks playground of about 0.11 acres, named for the East Flatbush community and for the original Dutch colonial settlement of Flatbush.
